- When sentiment is positive (≥0.20) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to capture sentiment-driven momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤-0.20) and forecast is rising, model often overestimates — reduce forecast slope or cap upward movement.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots in next 5–10 days — apply downward correction of 2–5% to avoid overreaction.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days falling after peak), model often fails to recognize — adjust forecast to reflect gradual decline, not linear continuation.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently underestimates true price peaks in early period (first 5–7 days) — increase forecast by 1–3% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or positive.
- If sentiment history shows repeated small positive spikes (e.g., 0.20, 0.00, 0.20), model often ignores — add small upward bias (0.5–1.5%) to forecast to capture sentiment clustering.
- When true outcome shows sharp drop after a peak, model often continues upward — apply “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
